The State Has No Business in Love: The Case for Abolishing Legal Marriage

Introduction

Marriage, as most of us encounter it, feels like a natural institution — ancient, essential, and inseparable from the fabric of organized society. We license it, regulate it, define it, and attach hundreds of legal consequences to it. But what if this arrangement is not only unnecessary but actively harmful? What if the government's entanglement with marriage is a relic that causes more problems than it solves?

This essay argues that the state should entirely cease recognizing, regulating, or privileging marriage. Not reform it. Not redefine it. Not expand or contract its boundaries. Abolish its legal status altogether — and allow human relationships to exist, contract, and organize themselves without government certification.

This position is not new. It has been advocated by libertarians, radical feminists, civil libertarians, and certain religious traditions. It is not an attack on love, commitment, or family. It is an argument that the state's role in certifying intimate relationships is incoherent, unjust, and increasingly indefensible.

I. The Historical Accident of State-Marriage Entanglement

To understand why state-licensed marriage should end, it helps to understand how it began — not as a principled policy choice, but as an accident of religious authority and bureaucratic convenience.

For most of Western history, marriage was a religious and familial institution. Churches and families managed it. The state had little involvement beyond inheritance disputes and property matters, which it handled through general contract and property law.

Government involvement expanded gradually. Marriage licenses emerged partly as tools of racial control — in the United States, they were used to enforce anti-miscegenation laws until Loving v. Virginia in 1967. Tax codes, immigration policy, and welfare systems built layer upon layer of legal consequences onto a single piece of paper. But no one ever conducted a rigorous cost-benefit analysis asking whether this entanglement served justice or merely compounded state power.

We inherited a system. We should not mistake inheritance for justification.

II. The Principle of Individual Liberty

The most fundamental argument is philosophical. In any society that claims to respect individual liberty, the default position should be that the state has no authority to certify, define, or regulate intimate personal relationships unless a compelling justification is offered.

What is that justification? Consider what a marriage license actually does. It does not create love. It does not ensure fidelity. It does not guarantee mutual support. What it does is create a legal status — a category into which the state places your relationship, with hundreds of attached rules you did not negotiate and may not even know about.

Many of those rules are defaults imposed without meaningful consent. Inheritance law, property division, medical decision-making, parental rights — all of these are bundled into a single take-it-or-leave-it package. You cannot unbundle them. You cannot customize them at the time of marriage without expensive legal instruments. The state offers you one template and calls it a universal institution.

This is extraordinary when you think about it. We would never accept this degree of paternalism in any other domain. Imagine if, when you opened a business, the state assigned you an unchangeable corporate structure with hundreds of default provisions you could not alter. We would recognize this as absurd. Yet this is precisely what marriage law does to intimate relationships.

Abolishing legal marriage does not abolish commitment. It returns relationship governance to the people in the relationship — where it belongs.

III. The Discrimination Problem Is Structural, Not Definitional

Much of the recent debate about marriage has focused on who can access it. But the deeper problem is not who is included or excluded — it is that the institution itself creates a privileged class of relationships.

Marriage confers over 1,000 federal legal benefits in the United States alone: tax advantages, immigration sponsorship, Social Security survivor benefits, hospital visitation rights, decision-making authority in medical emergencies, and more. These benefits are denied not only to same-sex couples (now resolved in many jurisdictions) but to an enormous range of committed relationships that do not fit the marriage template:

  • Elderly siblings who have lived together for decades and depend on each other.
  • Close friends who co-parent, share finances, and provide mutual care.
  • Platonic life partners who have built a household and want legal protections for their arrangement.
  • Polyamorous families of three or more committed adults raising children together.
  • Asexual romantic partners whose relationship is real and enduring but may not fit social expectations.

The state has no principled basis for deciding which of these relationships "count." Every attempt to define marriage inevitably privileges one model — historically, a heterosexual, monogamous, sexually exclusive dyad — and marginalizes all others. Even as the definition has been rightly expanded to include same-sex couples, the fundamental problem remains: the state is deciding which relationships matter.

The just solution is not to endlessly debate the boundaries of legal marriage. It is to remove the state from the business of certifying relationships entirely and make all legal protections available through general-purpose legal instruments.

IV. The Practical Alternative: Unbundling

"But what about hospital visitation? Inheritance? Medical decision-making?" These practical concerns are real — but they are arguments for better general-purpose legal tools, not for the continuation of state marriage.

Every legal benefit currently attached to marriage can be achieved through existing or easily creatable legal instruments:

Marriage Benefit Alternative Mechanism
Hospital visitation Healthcare proxy / designated visitor forms
Medical decision-making Medical power of attorney
Inheritance rights Wills, beneficiary designations
Tax benefits Reform tax law to stop penalizing or privileging household structures
Immigration sponsorship Relationship-based sponsorship independent of marital status
Child custody Parentage law, which can be separate from marriage law
Property division Partnership agreements, cohabitation contracts

None of these require the government to certify the nature of a relationship. They require only that individuals designate specific powers and rights to specific people. This is how we handle every other legal relationship in life. You do not need a "business marriage" to have a business partner — you need a contract. You do not need the state to certify your friendship to grant someone power of attorney. You simply sign a form.

The unbundling argument is powerful because it reveals that marriage law is not actually solving unique problems. It is bundling solutions to ordinary legal problems inside a culturally loaded institution — and then restricting that institution based on the state's preferences.

V. The Religious Freedom Argument

This argument cuts in an unexpected direction and has deep roots.

Many religious traditions regard marriage as a sacred covenant — a spiritual union that the state has no authority to create, dissolve, or define. When the state licenses marriage, it necessarily takes a position on what marriage is. Inevitably, that position conflicts with at least some religious views.

Conservative religious groups have argued that state redefinition of marriage (for example, to include same-sex couples) violates their religious understanding of the institution. Progressive religious groups have argued that state restrictions (such as historical bans on interracial marriage) violated their understanding. Both sides have a point: the moment the state defines marriage, it enters theological territory.

The cleanest solution — one that maximizes religious freedom for all traditions — is for the state to stop defining marriage entirely. Each religious community would be free to define, solemnize, and restrict marriage according to its own theology, with no legal consequences attached. The Catholic Church could recognize only marriages it considers valid. Quaker meetings could recognize any union they choose. The state would take no position, because it would have no marriage law.

This does not mean religious marriages would be meaningless. They would be deeply meaningful — to the people and communities that hold them sacred. What would change is that religious definitions would no longer carry state power, and state definitions would no longer carry theological implications.

VI. Feminist Critiques of State Marriage

The feminist tradition contains some of the most penetrating critiques of legal marriage — and they support abolition rather than reform.

Historically, marriage was a legal mechanism of women's subordination. Coverture laws merged a wife's legal identity into her husband's. She could not own property, sign contracts, or sue in her own name. While these overt provisions have been abolished, feminist scholars like Martha Fineman, Clare Chambers, and others have argued that marriage continues to structure gender inequality in subtler ways.

Marriage normalizes a particular model of care — one in which care is privatized within the household and disproportionately provided by women. The legal privileges of marriage incentivize this model: married couples receive tax benefits, health insurance coverage for spouses, and Social Security benefits for homemakers. Unmarried caregivers — disproportionately women caring for children, elderly parents, or disabled family members outside marriage — receive far less support.

State marriage, in this analysis, does not just reflect gender norms. It actively reinforces them by privileging one form of care relationship and making alternatives structurally disadvantageous.

Abolishing legal marriage would force a reckoning. If the state wants to support caregivers, it should support all caregivers — not only those who have obtained a government certificate for their romantic relationship.

VII. Addressing Counterarguments

"People need legal protection for their relationships."

Agreed. The argument is not for fewer legal protections but for different legal protections — ones available to everyone regardless of relationship structure, accessed through clear, specific legal instruments rather than bundled inside a single institution.

"Abolishing marriage would harm women and children."

The protections that currently flow through marriage can and should be available to everyone through general law. Child support, custody arrangements, and parental rights can be governed by parentage law, which is already largely independent of marriage. Protections against domestic violence exist in criminal and civil law outside of marriage. The question is whether these protections should be gated behind a marital status — and the answer is no.

"Marriage promotes social stability."

The evidence for this claim is contested. Many studies purporting to show that marriage causes positive outcomes suffer from severe selection effects — people who marry tend to be wealthier, healthier, and more educated to begin with. The causal arrow is unclear and may run entirely from stability to marriage rather than the reverse. Moreover, even if marriage did promote stability, that would be an argument for encouraging commitment, not for granting the state authority to certify and regulate it.

"This is just a libertarian fantasy."

The argument draws support from across the political spectrum. Libertarians make it from a perspective of individual liberty. Radicals and feminists make it from a perspective of gender justice. Religious traditionalists make it from a perspective of sacred autonomy. Civil libertarians make it from a perspective of state overreach. The coalition is unusual, but that reflects the strength of the argument, not its weakness.

VIII. A Vision of Freedom

Imagine a world where the state does not certify your most intimate relationships.

You choose whom to commit to. You decide — with your partner or partners — what your commitment means, how you share property, how you make medical decisions, how you raise children. You formalize those decisions through clear, specific legal tools: wills, powers of attorney, cohabitation agreements, parenting plans. If you are religious, your community blesses your union according to its own traditions. If you are not, you define your relationship on your own terms.

The state treats you as an individual. It does not ask whether you are married when you file your taxes, visit a hospital, sponsor an immigrant relative, or collect a deceased partner's benefits. It asks only whether you have the appropriate legal authorization for the action you are taking.

This is not a world without commitment. It is a world where commitment is voluntary, customizable, and free from state categorization. It is a world where the government stops pretending it knows what your relationship means — and lets you decide for yourself.

Conclusion

State marriage is a system born of religious inheritance, expanded by bureaucratic convenience, and sustained by cultural habit. It bundles ordinary legal protections inside a culturally loaded institution, privileges some relationships over others without principled justification, constrains individual liberty, entangles the state in theological territory, and reinforces gendered patterns of care.

Every function of marriage law can be better served by general-purpose legal instruments available to all. Every benefit can be unbundled. Every protection can be preserved.

What cannot be preserved is the state's authority to define, certify, and privilege one model of intimate life over all others. That authority was never legitimately earned. It should now be surrendered.

Abolish legal marriage. Not because love does not matter — but because it matters too much to be left to the state.
